title: Traffic Fraction Heuristics Lab — visual authoring for fractional rollouts
creator: Ava Bennett
description:
Goal: deliver a visual, low-friction builder for fractional traffic splits (canary/A-B experiments) that balances expressivity for power users with safety and clarity for non-engineers. The "Traffic Fraction Heuristics Lab" is a prototype space inside the Console where users can: compose fractional rollouts, preview expected telemetry windows, set safety bands and automated rollback triggers, and export a runtime-safe YAML spec that the orchestration layer can consume.

Scope: this ticket covers the high-fidelity flow prototype (Figma + interactive), a short PRD for UX constraints, and a moderated usability pass focused on the cognitive model for weighted splits and time-based ramps. Not in scope: runtime enforcement hooks and backend policy evaluation (these are owned by ENG-18742).

Design highlights and decisions to date:
1) Visual model: histogram + percentile slider — we keep the histogram of request volume by segment on the left and an editable curve on the right that represents the traffic fraction over time. Users can edit discrete points or drag a smooth curve to create ramps. Rationale: allows both precise percentage entry and quick gestural edits for rapid tuning.
2) Safety-first defaults: every new fractional rollout starts locked with a safety band (max exposure 2%, auto-hold for 15m by default) and an opt-in "confidence window" that requires X successful evals before growth. We debated forcing a lock vs. opt-out; decided opt-out to avoid blocking advanced workflows.
3) Telemetry preview: lightweight simulated panel shows projected CPU and token-cost delta, plus expected latency shift using model profiles. This data is a best-effort estimate and includes a disclaimer pointing to per-route historical dashboards.
4) Rollback UX: add an "emergency revert" CTA pinned to the top-right of the canvas with a one-click revert modal. For gradual rollbacks, users can drag the curve back to zero and apply immediately or schedule a taper. We opted for a guarded one-click revert with a short cooldown to avoid accidental flips.
5) Export & enforcement: prototype exports a linted YAML with stable keys the runtime can consume; export includes metadata fields (audience, burn-in policy, rollback policy). The format is intentionally simple to avoid coupling with future runtime schema changes.

Trade-offs discussed:
- Power vs. clarity: the curve editor is powerful but risks overwhelming non-technical product managers. Mitigation: add a "simple mode" that exposes only percent + duration presets and hides the curve.
- Predictive telemetry accuracy vs. user trust: pre-calculated deltas may diverge from production. Mitigation: surface confidence scores and link to live dashboards.
- Keyboard accessibility: curve drag interactions are not fully keyboard-friendly. We prototyped keyboard stepper controls as a fallback.

Next steps:
- Finish high-fidelity screens and handoff tokens to front-end (Rafael) by 2026-03-15.
- Sync with ENG-18742 on exported YAML schema and error modes (meeting scheduled 2026-03-05).
- Run 6 moderated usability sessions with PMs and SREs between 2026-03-08 and 2026-03-12; incorporate feedback.

Open questions for the triage meeting:
- Should "confidence windows" be modeled as an absolute count of requests or as a rolling success rate? (Trade-offs: count is simple; rate aligns with quality signals.)
- Do we expose audience targeting at the same level as fraction editing or keep it in a separate "Audience" tab?

Acceptance criteria:
- Figma prototype implements curve editor + simple mode + telemetry preview.
- Exported YAML schema approved by ENG-18742 and validated by a unit test.
- Usability score >= 80% on the "set a safe canary" task in moderated sessions.
